URL: https://ryanbigg.com/2026/10/leaving-tech, See on Hacker News

I’ve now applied for over 3 dozen jobs and I’ve heard back from 24 of them with a rejection. This tech market at the moment is so very cooked and for that reason I’m stepping away from tech.

I’ve been a developer for 20 years across more than just the Ruby and JavaScript that I’m known for. I’ve written books about programming, I’ve given talks and I’ve ran events. I maintain two of the most downloaded Ruby packages. And yes, I delivered the fuck out of value for shareholders. I also grew a team from 2 people to 12 people at my last job.

I cannot continue to put myself through this process of rejection. It is causing me a great deal of mental harm and anguish.

The industry at the moment wants people who know how to use AI to further the business goals but here’s the thing nobody wants to admit: not one person knows how to use AI to actually do that. I use it to write a lot of my code and then I critically review that code before it reaches production.

My life is based here in Warrnambool and I choose to work remotely from here. Hybrid is infeasible even if it were in Melbourne because Melbourne is 3.5hrs away on the train. I know I can work remotely effectively because I did it for the last 6 years. And I helped others adjust to that as well!

So it’s clear that there’s no room for me in tech anymore, so I’m going to chat to some people to figure out what’s next.

item.title: I turned my unused Kindle into a photo frame with GPT-6 Astra (137 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nirajrajgor.com/blog/kindle-photo-frame-with-ai, See on Hacker News

My Kindle was sitting unused, so I decided to see whether AI could help me find a new use for it. I wanted to create a custom app that could cover a range of uses and be controlled by an AI agent on my MacBook.

I started with a small goal: use my own image as the Kindle's screensaver. Once that worked, I asked the agent to build an app that could cycle through a collection of photos.

We called the project KindleCTL. On my Kindle, I open "Photo Slideshow" from the same screen where I choose my books. It cycles through ten photos, showing each for four minutes. When I want to read, I exit the slideshow and return to my books.

I used Codex and T3 Code on my Mac to work with the coding agents.

I first tried GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning effort set to Extra High. It wrote code to connect to the Kindle but couldn't resolve an error that prevented it from storing data on the device. Then I tried Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, but Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards blocked each attempt after two prompts. Finally, I tried GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to High. We were able to jailbreak the Kindle.

We used the existing jailbreak code as a reference to build our own tools for running custom software on the Kindle. Then we created and installed the slideshow app.

The slideshow passed its automated checks on my Mac, but switching photos on the Kindle left traces of the previous image on screen. The tests hadn't caught how the physical display refreshed. Getting from passing tests to something I could use turned out to be the most interesting part of the experiment.

Let's walk through how we went from an unused Kindle to a working photo frame, starting with getting the agent connected.

Connecting the agent to the Kindle

I started in an empty project folder with a 10th-generation Kindle Basic. I gave the agent its network address and device details. We had no USB connection, so the entire setup happened over Wi-Fi.

From there, we still needed to set up access to run our own software on the Kindle.

The GPT-5.6 Sol attempt got as far as loading a helper on the Kindle, but the program that helper was meant to start never reported that it was ready to execute. It couldn't locate a filesystem where it could store content.

The attempts with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were both blocked by Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards after two prompts. Then I tried GPT-6 Astra. I explicitly asked it to build the custom software we needed for personal use and take inspiration from existing open-source projects.

We adapted the existing jailbreak from SpiderCat, released by sparklerfish and the KindleModding community, and built custom tools called KindleCTL around it.

  • What we built: Tools to send commands from my Mac, transfer files, and investigate errors on the Kindle.
  • What broke: Our launcher crashed before it could start. We traced that to a compatibility issue with the Kindle's older system software and fixed how the launcher was built.
  • How we checked: We connected with administrator access, transferred files both ways, and displayed text. Later, we verified that access still worked after a reboot.

The feedback loop was the game changer

Initially, the agent could connect to the Kindle but couldn't display data. To debug this, it asked me for pictures of the Kindle's screen. I took photos with my phone and shared them with the agent on my Mac.

This was becoming tedious. Since the agent was connected to the Kindle, I wondered why it couldn't get this information itself. I asked it to set up a feedback loop so it could access logs without me having to share screenshots.

The agent set up a persistent diagnostic connection so it could collect errors and test fixes without asking me to download and reopen a package each time. Later, we added remote screen captures so it could also inspect what the Kindle was displaying.

This was a turning point that let the agent continue implementing changes on autopilot. Its reasoning traces showed it figuring out which folders survived a restart and which could store external data.

I was surprised the agent hadn't suggested this on its own. Once I asked for a feedback loop, it set one up and could test fixes without my help.

Most of the code was written in Python. The Kindle's launcher and slideshow were written in C, with shell scripts handling installation and device controls.

With the connection working, I asked the agent to try a small test first: transfer an image and set it as the Kindle's screensaver. I checked that the image appeared correctly and that waking the Kindle brought back the normal Home screen. Once that worked, I asked for the slideshow app.

Getting the slideshow working

I asked the agent for a looping slideshow of ten photos, with an Exit button. Each photo would fit the screen while keeping its original aspect ratio.

The slides were changing, but the transitions weren't smooth, so I asked the agent to look into it. With the feedback loop already in place, it investigated the issue and used the Kindle's built-in screen refresh mechanism to clear the previous image after each slide change.

The screen captures showed complete images, but they couldn't reveal traces left on the physical display. After the refresh change, I checked the Kindle and confirmed that each photo looked clean.

I customized how long each photo stays on screen and the brightness level. If the Kindle goes to sleep, the slideshow picks up where it left off when it wakes.

For now, I use my Mac to change the photos and slideshow timing. The photos stay stored on the Kindle, so the slideshow works without Wi-Fi. In the future, we could add controls to change the slideshow timing on the Kindle and send photos directly from a phone or another device.

What I learned

Next time, I'd set up the feedback loop from the start so the agent could read logs, inspect screen captures, and test fixes on the device.

The Kindle now sits on our wooden shelf, where we use it every day as a photo frame.

I started because I was curious about what AI could help me do with an unused device. Now I have an app for my photos that works the way I asked, plus the tools to keep experimenting with the Kindle.

Disclaimer: This was a personal experiment on my own Kindle, not a step-by-step jailbreak guide. Only experiment with devices you own or have explicit permission to modify.

item.title: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. (303 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://yyhh.org/blog/2026/10/ai-is-a-tool/, See on Hacker News

In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

item.title: Who Is Vfmaddrnd231pd? (155 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://purplesyringa.moe/blog/who-is-vfmaddrnd231pd/, See on Hacker News

October 12, 2026

vfmaddrnd231pd is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like vfmadd231pd, but here rnd means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as:

VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control

[…] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3).

Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But vfmaddrnd231pd allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster.

Or so it would, if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics _mm_fmaddround_pd and _mm256_fmaddround_pd that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue:

VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib

VEX is the VEX prefix, but what is DDS? This opcode is the only mention of DDS in the SDM, and this SO answer says that DDS is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises #UD (“UnDefined instruction”)!

I already found it strange that the SDM only lists vfmaddrnd231pd and not other variants like using pd/ps/sd/ss or 132/213/231, which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version.

I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the vfmaddrnd* set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that.

If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer.

item.title: Making big downloads resumable in Firefox (142 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lunarwatcher.codeberg.page/til/firefox/resumable-big-downloads.html, See on Hacker News

firefox

For whatever reason, Firefox 28 and newer (i.e. every modern version after like 2014) ships with network.http.response.timeout set to 300 seconds. This seems to interfere with resuming big downloads, as well as the general stability of big downloads.

Setting network.http.response.timeout to 0 (or something very big) in about:config seems to make big downloads both resumable and at least a little more stable. I don't understand why this works, but experimental testing supports it.

Note that this assumes the server supports resumable downloads; if it doesn't, no settings in firefox or any other browser are going to help. However, the problem this fixes is firefox being unable to resume a resumable download on error. I don't entirely know if this is the case, but it experimentally looks like resumable downloads in firefox rely on connection timeouts rather than the .part files they download. Firefox will happily ignore an existing .part without this option, and I do not understand why.

Resumable downloads in firefox generally appear to be fairly unstable though. This has been a known problem in some form since as far back as 2005. I also found that there's a manual .part shuffle to make firefox actually resume downloads, but I'm not doing that shit. As a non-firefox workaround, using wget -c -O "$filename" "$url" also works, and wget overall appears to be fairly stable.

I do also suspect firefox does some hidden retries if it can before it considers the download to have failed - from some experimental testing, it does appear that this is at least partly related to network.http.response.timeout, and that exceeding the timeout interferes with this process.

I have not attempted to confirm any of this with FF's source code, because I have no clue where to look.

item.title: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default (509 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48195, See on Hacker News

What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex, Linux (WSL2)

What feature would you like to see?

Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false) for the CLI, or at least ask once before turning it on.

Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session:

  1. Starts a persistent background daemon (codex app-server --managed-daemon). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot.
  2. Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex, codex-code-mode-host, bundled bwrap/zsh/rg) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager.
  3. Starts a detached updater (codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969).
  4. Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457 and Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537 (daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause.

For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap.

If it stays on by default, please at least:

  • exit an auto-started daemon when its last client disconnects;
  • not copy/self-update when the CLI was installed by a package manager (npm/brew/pacman) — run the installed binary instead (Support externally managed app-server daemon executables #41188, npm update leaves app-server on old version, but daemon update/restart refuse recovery #46468, Codex 0.157.0 no longer starts with the Arch Linux package unless --no-daemon is used #48050).

Additional information

Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually).

Workaround I'm using:

codex features disable daemon_auto_start
codex app-server daemon stop
pkill -f 'app-server daemon pid-update-loop'   # not stopped by `daemon stop`
rm -rf ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon

With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon.

Related: #40969, #41188, #46468, #48050, #42457, #37537

item.title: Publishers Killed the Paperback, Then Blamed Readers (117 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jacobin.com/2026/10/books-publishing-reading-mass-market-paperback, See on Hacker News

It seems every week a new piece about the decline and fall of the American reading habit goes viral. The idea that we’re entering a literary apocalypse that threatens to destabilize our democracy is perhaps overstated, but nobody is denying the book-reading trend is grim. In the most recent international assessment of adult skills, conducted in 2023, 28 percent of American adults scored at or below the lowest level of literacy — up from 19 percent just six years earlier. By one widely cited estimate, more than half of American adults read below a sixth-grade level.

It’s interesting to note that these hand-wringing, sky-is-falling pieces unfailingly focus on external issues. Few of us doubt what we feel in our bones to be true — that long-form reading is being harmed by disruptive technologies and other beyond-our-control societal issues (political dysfunction and a decrepit educational system) that apply to the demand side of the equation.

But what about the supply side? Could it be that corporatized publishing — with all of its consolidations and centralization — may have enshittified the product to the point where it has abetted the decline in consumer demand?

Consider the death of the mass-market paperback last year. When the Big Five publishing houses (Penguin Random House, Macmillan, HarperCollins, Hachette, and Simon & Schuster) took the most affordable book format in America — known for its modest price and compact size — off of life support in 2025, it had long ago failed to live up to the “mass” part of its name. At that point, the books under that banner were recognizable but lacking the vitality and freshness that had first driven them to national attention in the twentieth century.

Until the 1940s, book retail was dominated by hardcovers — books held between cloth- or paper-covered boards, the pages secured by sewn spines. Penguin in the UK and Pocket Books here in the United States were the first to make successful use of an alternative book format that rivaled — and, for many decades, far outsold — the hardback. This cheaper-to-manufacture book had a soft cover and relied upon a glued (versus stitched) binding. The resulting tome was easier to carry and much easier to afford. The new format was as much commercial opportunism as it was any attempt to democratize reading or to improve the citizenry’s understanding of the world. If you make a dime on each purchase of one hundred thousand paperbacks, that’s more than making a buck each on 2,500 hardcovers, which was the average unit sale back then. Better yet, these books were sold all over middle America — in drugstores, grocery stores, and gas stations — not just in the little metropolitan oases.

In the post–Great Depression years, American bookstores were hardly ubiquitous. Large metro areas with a sufficient intelligentsia density might have a few, but in the 1930s there were only about five hundred dedicated bookshops across all of America. At the same time, basic literacy was nearly universal — by the 1930 census, some 96 percent of Americans over the age of ten could read and write — but the average American only knew books through schools (which used to buy a lot more books than they do now), libraries (which used to contain a lot more books than they do now), and catalogs (which used to sell a lot more books than they do now). Unless you lived in an affluent area with a bookstore or were near a department store or gift shop — which also sometimes had small book sections — you simply did not encounter them as a working adult.

But when these cheap little books dubbed “mass-market paperbacks” began showing up, they were a hit. America’s Pocket Books launched in 1939 and sold 8.5 million copies within two years. Which is even more remarkable considering they were not yet being sold “north of Boston, west of Chicago, or south of Washington [DC].” The books were averaging close to one hundred thousand units each, with a population a little over a third the size of today’s United States. When the industry discontinued the format in 2024, the highest-selling new mass-market title — a Danielle Steel book — sold 53,000 units. It’s no wonder the executives decided to scuttle the whole thing and to blame the customer for it.

One of the bigger recent pieces on the supposed new trend in anti-literacy was an Atlantic piece called “The End of Reading Is Here,” and it was typical in its emphasis on the failures of the society that is degenerating outside the walls of the Big Five. The piece gives us the history of publishing from Mesopotamia to Ptolemy to Johannes Gutenberg and emphasizes the importance that our nation’s founders and civil war heroes placed on long-form print.

Marshall McLuhan, Neil Postman, Walter J. Ong, and Alexander Luria are name-checked. The tech-happy media and educational industries are decried, and the system that allows kids to spend 4.5 hours a day on social media is called out, but nowhere in the massive piece is any shade thrown at the book publishing industry with whom The Atlantic, for 169 years, has been cozy, and to which the article’s Yale-educated writer likely — as with most staff writers — means to sell manuscripts over the course of a career.

There is plenty of good reason for gloom. We are told that 80 percent of elementary school teachers report that their students have, by kindergarten, received school-issued personal video devices. But the Atlantic piece contains no implication that one possible reason books and long-form reading are falling away, a theoretically contributory factor to the mass market’s extinction and the plummeting demand for books, involves the supply-side of the equation. Any thought that what the publishing industry is printing, or how it has been pricing it, or where it has been placing it, just might have harmed our nation’s reading habit is never mentioned. The writer has good company in blaming the people on the outside. None of the publishing executives and pundits that attended the mass-market paperback’s funeral ceremonies last year did any self-implication either.

“We follow the consumer,” said Dennis Abboud, CEO of ReaderLink, America’s largest book distributor, upon announcing the death of the mass-market paperback. “It seems the consumer has spoken,” said Steve Zacharius, CEO of one of the biggest publishers in the format. “As a format, I would say it’s pretty much over,” said Ivan Held of Penguin Random House. All this shrugging and hand-washing for the book format that, as one regretful publisher eloquently put it, saved (or at least forestalled the decline of) America. “I believe that mass-market paperbacks democratized America,” said Esther Margolis of Newmarket Press. “For basically the equivalent of a dollar or two, you know, you could be educated. You could pick them up at the school book fair. You could pick them up at a local gas station . . . You didn’t have to be an elitist.”

But could the mega-consolidated Big Five American publishing industry bear any blame for this state of affairs?

Consumer scientists have long understood that that popular habits are not just among the hardest things to break but are also very difficult to make. Many companies try to integrate their products into preexisting habits, but it’s rare that a company touches off an entirely new one, much less one at the scale of the mass-market paperback. Those 8.5 million paperbacks sold by Pocket Books from 1939 to 1941 were arguably proof of a bigger, more instantaneous habit birth than that of even the iPhone, which sold a comparable amount of their own product but to a population that had grown three times larger.

But America’s decades-long mass-market paperback binge (which in 1979 topped out at 387 million annual units sold) suggests that we, as a people, are capable of — and perhaps even prone to — falling into a book-reading habit. So was there anything publishers could have done to prevent the death of the mass-market paperback and the decline of our national reading habit?

In 1939, television didn’t exist, movies lasted only a couple hours — versus the days you can occupy through a single book — and even there you were stuck with whatever was playing at the non-multiplex cinema. You also had at best a dozen radio stations to choose from versus the cheap time-killing options we have on this side of the digital revolution.

The new landscape obviously comprises external demand-affecting features that exist beyond the reach of even the most powerful book industry executive. And judging whether books are more or less attractive seems like a hard one to quantify. Proving that publishers have gotten better or worse at designing attractive book jackets, executing motivating marketing campaigns, and delivering compelling manuscripts would doubtless be largely subjective.

But one aspect of appeal for which it is much easier to hold the publishers’ feet to the fire is range. There is a bigger story to be told here, but let’s take a snapshot and consider the first ten mass-market paperbacks that Pocket Books published:

Emily Brontë, Bambi, Dorothy Parker, Agatha Christie, Shakespeare, a Victorian bildungsroman and a Pulitzer Prize–winning novel by Thornton Wilder. That’s quite a broad spectrum! Now let’s hold this mini-catalog up against the mass-market bestsellers list from the very month in 2025 that Dennis Abboud, CEO of ReaderLink — a former managing partner at a private equity firm — announced that the mass-market paperback was to be put out to pasture:

Comparing the first ten paperbacks ever published — which sold millions of copies in a very different world — to the last ten is not entirely unfair. Those were the industry’s ten priority titles of 1939; the latter ones are the ten priority titles of the industry eighty-six years later. In other words, decisions — curations, really — made by the companies. The former are effectively the ten books a person of 1939 was most likely to have encountered while shopping, and the latter are the ten books a person is most likely to have encountered while doing the same in February 2025. In 1939, we have adventure books, plays, poems, a story about a deer, a murder mystery, a prize-winning literary novel, and a movie tie-in — all by a set of authors ranging in age, if they were living at time of publication, from thirty-eight to sixty-nine. In 2025, we have only contemporary commercial fiction options, half of which are series titles (one of which had a whopping thirty-five prior installments) and by eight brand-name authors, average age seventy-four, plus two whose franchise author is a man who would have been eighty-six at the time of publication, at least had he not died in 2004.

There’s nothing wrong with pursuing safe bets: all these old brand authors and their long-established readerships are obviously dependable, at least from a quarterly earnings standpoint, versus Pocket Books’ unscientific, consumer-data-lacking, instinct-driven — albeit extremely successful — strategy from 1939. But given that variety is an important part of attracting consumers, is it possible our twenty-first century publishers have diminished the wider appeal of their product — for readers and potential readers outside the dependable boomer commercial-fiction core — even just a little bit?

As to affordability, ¢25 (the price of each of Pocket Books’ titles) went a lot further in 1939 than it does now but was still a consumer-friendly price point. It was just slightly higher than what our great-great-grandparents would have paid for a gallon of gas and slightly lower than what they’d have paid for a dozen eggs. In 2024, the format’s last year of full national distribution, a new mass-market paperback would set you back three times as much as a dozen eggs or a gallon of gas.

One might suspect that materials, distribution, or other book-specific costs had risen over the intervening decades. But how then to explain that the mass-market paperback’s older sibling — the hidebound hardcover — hasn’t seen an inflation nearly so dramatic? Today’s hardback novel has a cover price between $28 and $32. That’s 40 percent cheaper than it would have been back in the 1940s, and this is before a typical national retailer discount of more than 20 percent (and often up to 50 percent) for best-selling titles. In 1939, you could buy ten mass-market paperbacks for the cost of a single new hardback. In 2024, you could barely buy two. Which means that under the leadership of the Big Five and their equally hegemonic national retail partners, the flagship product favored by elite-facing bookstores in wealthy enclaves got cheaper, and the format with the proven mass potential got many times more expensive.

Finally, let’s consider availability. Even before the mass-market paperback was discontinued, books were being carried in fewer and fewer places. Supermarkets, drugstores, truck stops, newsstands, and department stores,had all gotten out of the business. And the bookselling stalwarts of recent decades have been faltering too. In 2024, Costco, which used to sell millions of units a year, stopped carrying books in most of its stores. The big national book retailer Borders, with an assist from private equity, went out of business in 2011. Barnes & Noble has been roughly holding steady, but it has just around six hundred outlets in at best 19 percent of our nation’s counties.

The trends the publishers and the media cite to justify this availability crisis are real. But were they unavoidable? And are they excusable? And are they perhaps also driven by problems the two other As — appeal and affordability — over which the industry has even more direct control? Could and should the US publishing industry in fact be visibly exploring solutions or putting up a public fight to maintain a more significant non-digital distribution of its titles? Could and should the industry notice that the mass-market paperback is still for sale in Canada — where, in that same 2023 assessment, just 18 percent of adults scored at or below the lowest literacy level, compared with 28 percent here — and at a price less than half of what it rose to in the United States?

It’s difficult to see how the corporatized, highly centralized industry is walking away blameless from killing off one of its former darlings — the affordable paperback. Clearly it’s easier to focus on fewer higher-income readers than on a multitude of Americans whose lives you have no social connection to. Clearly decisions were made — ones that no doubt have had a major effect on American reading habits. And clearly the highly intertwined media establishment is not going to second-guess them.

But maybe you should.

item.title: Just say no to OpenAI and Anthropic (157 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://micahflee.com/just-say-no-to-openai-and-anthropic/, See on Hacker News

I recently read End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. It's an excellent book and I highly recommend that everyone read it. Tech oligarchs make up an important component of the end-times-fascist coalition. One thing that stood out to me, as a software and security engineer who finds LLMs to be extremely powerful, is that the American frontier labs are run by unhinged lunatics who genuinely believe they're creating the Machine God, that they're fine with burning down the world to bring about AGI, and that they believe with religious fervor that they're the only ones smart enough to safely control it. I already kind of knew this, but this book really made it sink in.

As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they're not. They're not the only companies doing this work. In fact, a lot of the open weight models are just about as good as the latest ChatGPT and Claude models, including for incredibly complex tasks like vulnerability research.

Unlike models from OpenAI and Anthropic, open weight models have major advantages:

  • It's possible to run them privately on your own hardware (if you can somehow get a computer with enough RAM)
  • You can use a provider like Tinfoil that relies on secure enclaves to run them privately (I talk about this in a bit more detail below)
  • If privacy isn't a huge concern, you can use any number of other providers, some of them quite affordable, and it's easy to switch so you're not locked into a single evil vendor
  • You can still use powerful LLMs without financially supporting deranged oligarchs who gamble with life on Earth so that they can always remain in power

ChatGPT and Claude will never be private

These companies only offer closed versions of their powerful models (despite the word "open" in "OpenAI"). You pay them for chat and/or API access, and they are allowed to look at everything you do.

They offer a checkbox so you can opt out of them using your data for training, but your chat sessions still aren't private. They have access to it all. They can look at it, share it with governments or companies, or do whatever they want. It's possible, likely even, that they won't use it for training if you've opted out, at least not right now. But do you really trust that long-term? Have they done anything to make anyone believe that they respect people's data?

OpenAI and Anthropic are corporate gatekeepers

Their models have strict guardrails, as anyone who's tried to use them for anything cybersecurity-related has no doubt noticed.

Every session has a cop agent reading your transcript over your shoulder, making sure you're not using it for hacking. If it thinks you might be, the cop agent stops your session from continuing. It's very strict, and false positives happen all the time. Of course, not everyone has the cop watching them.

Some people get access to the models with looser restrictions or with none at all. OpenAI has Trusted Access for Cyber and Anthropic has the Cyber Verification Program. To gain access to more capable, less policed versions of their models, individuals and companies need to apply and be approved by OpenAI and Anthropic. A lot of US cybersecurity companies get access. Almost certainly US military contractors do too, and probably any parts of the US government that want it.

While there's some merit in restricting powerful models, handing the ultimate power to decide who gets access to them to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei – with consultation from the Trump Administration, of course – is a terrible, undemocratic idea.

I think a better approach is to simply not put yourself in a situation where you rely on ChatGPT or Claude. Instead of begging corporate overlords for privileged access, it's better to spend your time figuring out how to get models like GLM-5.3 to meet your needs. And it's not hard. These models are good, with the added benefit that they don't have a cop watching over your shoulder!

Open weight models are impressive

So far, open weight models seem to be about four months behind the fancy proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Four months is nothing.

I'm extremely impressed right now with GLM-5.3. There's plenty of data and benchmarks out there, but my vibes-based opinion from using it is that it's basically on par with Claude Opus 5.5 for software engineering.

I'm also impressed with GLM-5.3-Flash. This is similar to Claude Opus 4.8. It's much smaller and cheaper than GLM-5.3, and still incredibly capable. It's also actually feasible for an individual person to get hardware to run it, like if you can one day get your hands on a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM.

GLM models are made by a Chinese company called Z.ai. While the models are impressive, I don't recommend making an account directly with Z.ai or sending them any of your data. Their coding harness ZCode (their version of Claude Code) was recently caught silently uploading local source code repos and sending them back to Alibaba Cloud without consent. Also, it's safe to assume that Chinese companies will share any data you provide to them with the Chinese government.

Other open weight models from Chinese companies that are impressive include the DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi families of models. It's perfectly fine, safe, and secure to use these open weight models. Just don't trust the companies themselves with your chat sessions.

Another frontier AI lab worth a look is Mistral. As a French company, it's the only big player that's not Chinese or American. They just released an open weight frontier model called Mistral Large 4, aka Le Chonk. I think it's quite a bit more reasonable to trust Mistral with your data compared to the Chinese or American companies.

Private inference with Tinfoil or Maple AI

It's possible to have private AI, even without hosting it locally yourself, using secure enclaves. These aren't perfect, but I do think they provide a very meaningful difference in privacy compared to the status quo mode, which is "the provider can access everything with no restrictions."

The company that's doing the most work here is Tinfoil. If you want to learn the details, read their docs on secure enclaves and remote attestation. Another company doing this is Maple AI – although, technically, Maple uses Tinfoil for inference in the background.

Both Tinfoil and Maple are good options. Tinfoil is cheaper, but Maple is more consumer-focused.

If you want a ChatGPT-like experience, where you can talk to a chatbot, have it look stuff up for you on the internet, give it access to docs to read or do stuff with, access it in a mobile app, etc., then I'd go with Maple. There's a small free plan and a Pro plan that costs $20/month.

If you want to do real agentic coding tasks like software engineering, reverse engineering, malware analysis, CTFs or pen tests, etc., then you should use Tinfoil instead. They charge by the token for private inference, so no monthly plan. GLM-5.3 currently costs $1.80 per 1M input tokens, $0.80 per 1M cached tokens, and $5.75 per 1M output tokens. You can use significantly fewer tokens if you choose the "low" reasoning level, and it's still very impressive.

Inference without the privacy

If you don't want to pay a premium for private inference from Tinfoil or Maple, but you still want to free yourself from OpenAI and Anthropic, there are tons of less-private options that are also very cheap.

One that I've been playing with is OpenCode Go. It costs $10/month for more than $10 worth of credits. This is an inference router, which basically means your API queries do something like this: your computer -> OpenCode Go API -> the actual inference provider. This means that both OpenCode Go and whatever backend provider they're using will have access to your session data. That said, the privacy section of their docs promises which models data won't be used for training (most of them) and what the data retention is (zero days for most, including all the GLM, Qwen, Kimi, and DeepSeek models). Of course, it's just a promise. Nothing technical guarantees it.

There are plenty of other cheap options out there for non-private inference, if you just want to experiment with powerful open weight models.

How I'm using these models

I've been using both Tinfoil and OpenCode Go, configured with my current harness of choice, OpenCode. I've been mostly using GLM-5.3 on low reasoning, with great results. (Things change so quickly with the open weight models, who knows what will be best six months from now.)

I use OpenCode Go inference for completely public work, like when I'm implementing something that's already open source.

I use Tinfoil for everything else.

I've only just started working this way, but so far, I think the open weight models can easily completely replace my use of ChatGPT and Claude, at a comparable or cheaper price, with the added benefit that they're far more private and there are far fewer guardrails.

item.title: 'AI' Is Not a Tool by Rich Hickey (246 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/ai-tool-rich-hickey-kjl8e, See on Hacker News

(I keep delivering this as a quip, here's a bit more)

First order of business - is 'tool' going to have an interesting, distinguishing and thus illuminative meaning or be a mere platitudinous stand-in for "anything useful"?

We'll save tool as "anyone/thing that can be exploited" for the AI titans, for whom VCs, politicians, wannabe-titan-CEOs, software devs, rural towns etc are all 'tools'. The pockets on the front of my shirts are useful (I need to keep my reading glasses handy), but they are not tools. Similarly, fast food drive-thru windows are useful, but are not tools (more later).

Some definitions of 'tool':

  • a device or implement, especially one held in the hand, used to carry out a particular function
  • an instrument (such as a hammer or saw) used or worked by hand : an instrument used by a handicraftsperson or laborer in their work

What I like best - A tool is something you wield.

  • wield - to use (as a tool or instrument) especially with full command or power : handle, manipulate, control

Especially useful in that are:

  • Held in your hand - a source of both control and feedback, and an indication of the intimacy of the act of use
  • Power - force, energy transmission and direction, leverage etc
  • Control - intention and continuous directing of the course of events

Tools are implements with which you do something, they do not do things for you. Tool use builds, rewards, and often requires, expertise and skill. The continuous application of technique and energy, and sensory feedback, are essential to the buildup of expertise (from experiri - "try").

Good tools have many properties LLMs lack - they are predictable, reliable, deterministic, of bounded function, hopefully simple etc.

What you learn while wielding a tool is something about the world, the task, the physics, logic etc of what you are trying to do or the situation you are trying to overcome. And often, something about yourself.

As a lifelong tool builder and user, I know what tools are. LLMs are not tools.

Control, sensory feedback, intention, intimacy, continuous direction, expertise etc are all missing from LLM use. LLMs are not wielded. LLMs are automation.

  • automation - (of a device or process) working by itself with little or no direct human control.

A drive-thru is not a tool for cooking, it is automation for avoiding cooking. LLMs are not tools with which you write code - they are automation with which you avoid writing code, to which you abdicate writing code.

You don't direct the action of an LLM - you make requests and it acts on its own, without your energy or continuous direction. This request/automation cycle is not wielding, it's not control, it's not continuous, it's without feedback.

What you are doing while using automation, instead of learning real-world truths, is attempting to divine the details du jour of some automaton. And striving to game them - e.g. ordering a custom burger (no onions) in order to get a freshly made one. Or filling voodoo.md with just the right incantations. You are only a software update from everything you've 'learned' being rendered obsolete by the latest algorithm. (A soggy cold burger from which the onions have been removed) You have traded working with the world to working for a capricious robot.

It is a mistake to be haphazard about "tools" being equivalent to utility, e.g. saying - "the LLM didn't write my paper, I just used it as a tool to read and summarize some research papers". But you didn't wield it to read those papers (as you might a Kindle). It read the papers, not you.

What do you miss by abdicating doing the reading? Pretty much everything. First and foremost, you miss learning how to write from those who can. You miss learning how to formulate an argument. You miss noticing things. You miss loading your background mind with fodder for novel ideas. You miss building trust in some authors and suspicion of others. You miss all the jokes. You miss all of the edges. You miss learning how to think.

Tools don't get "misaligned", they don't "go rogue", they don't "escape containment", "conspire" etc.

LLMs are not tools. I know many people use the phrase "just tools" simply to indicate "they are what you make of them". Except that's not true. Automation has intrinsic properties and differences from tools that you ignore at your peril.

Rich

item.title: Feds got warrants to use fake cell towers to hunt down Don Lemon's producer (164 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.wired.com/story/feds-got-warrants-to-use-fake-cell-towers-to-hunt-down-don-lemons-producer/, See on Hacker News

US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.

The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.

Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”

Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.

The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.

Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.

The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.

“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.

Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.

The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.

The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.

The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.

DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.

The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.

While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.

A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record

Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.

In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”

The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.

The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.

These lines are very difficult for me to write because I feel like digging my own grave. AI systems are improving by leaps and bounds. From the early 2022 fumbling release of ChatGPT, which couldn’t correctly count the number of a’s in my name (it claimed two), we reached OpenAI’s release of math papers where an internal AI model solved many hundreds of previously open math problems. Aside from philosophical arguments, practical claims regarding the superiority of human thought, on grounds such as hallucinations or bias, increasingly appear to me like rearguard defence. For the bulk of today’s cognitive work, the writing’s on the wall: AI will take over.

The three factors driving AI’s dominance in the modern work environment are better performance, lower cost, and higher availability. The performance of AI models is rising spectacularly on all fronts: perception, knowledge processing and creation, reasoning, judgement, and autonomous action. In parallel, human proficiency in key information-processing skills, low on average among adults, is even declining among students. Consequently, AI systems are performing better than humans in ever-wider range of tasks.

AI’s cost is also falling due to huge investments and scientific progress. Successive generations of AI models offer superior performance at lower cost, with older models retained only for backward compatibility. As a result, it is making financial sense to replace or augment human labour with AI systems across an increasingly broad range of activities.

Finally, and most obviously, AI systems can operate around the clock, without the need for rest or breaks. They can also help alleviate labour shortages arising from demographic trends or skills gaps. Meanwhile, trillions of dollars in projected data centre investment through 2030 are set to bring vast additional AI processing capacity online.

As happened in past technological revolutions, there will undoubtedly be fierce resistance to the replacement of cognitive work with AI. This time it will be fiercer because, unlike previous revolutions, which transformed manual labour, AI challenges knowledge workers, whose specialised expertise, control over information, and decision-making authority afford them greater economic and organisational power. Governments will try to clip AI’s wings through regulation and taxation. Such actions didn’t quell past revolutions so there’s little reason to believe they’ll work now.

So what’s the fate of human thought? My take is that cognitive work will diminish. Thought will increasingly become a leisure pursuit, as hunting did following animal domestication, calligraphy after typography, woodworking after industrialisation, and horse riding after motorisation. Machines transformed much of physical activity from necessity into choice; similarly, AI will decouple human thinking from its economic purpose.

I’ll end with my thoughts on how to prepare for and live through this transition. My take is that building this AI-driven world, riding through the bumps along the road, and preparing to live a fulfilling and satisfying life in an environment where AI dominates cognitive work will be hugely demanding, stressful, and intellectually challenging. Such is the nature of revolutions. Consequently, we must keep pace with and capitalise on AI’s advances; be flexible, adaptable, and resilient; and build a purposeful and rewarding life beyond work. My challenge ahead is to move from making a living by thinking, to making thinking part of a life worth living.

A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish.

Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers.

Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse, and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse.

Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence

Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier.

When we introduced Muse Spark, we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.

Frontier Capabilities

Model Highlights

The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.

The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite.

For more details about our evaluations, see our report.

The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding.

Domain Expertise

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.

Active Memory

One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory: carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.

Active Focus

Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects.

Frontier Coding

Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process.

Capabilities That Generalize

Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture.

To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”).

Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training.

Safety at the Frontier

Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information.

As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework.

Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon.

We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come.

# Corey Prophitt » A modern web app in c

## INTRO

If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology.

Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript.

Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026.

## TLDR

CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026.

You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head.

## HOW IT WAS DONE

The stack is BCHS: OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite.

There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds.

There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly.

There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API.

There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder.

Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary.

OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem.

I lean on three additional libraries:

  • libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark.
  • libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks.
  • libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark.

Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium.

  • libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies.
  • SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build.

Both are vendored and built as part of the project.

The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second.

Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory.

## WHAT I LIKED

Fundamentals over frameworks.

CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since.

There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts:

  • Request headers.
  • Request methods.
  • Query strings.
  • Body data.

If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI.

It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever.

Clear separation of concerns.

A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic.

CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what.

It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb.

In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills).

Minimal supply chain risk.

With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies.

Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015.

My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019.

Simple tooling.

I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters, and no AI.

Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile.

Open a file, read it, and you know what it does.

Great tooling is within reach.

When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C.

The maturity goes further than the tools themselves: integration is built into many editors. Vim ships with native support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug).

Writing HTML and CSS in C isn't too bad.

I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined.

All too many times have I:

  • Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax.
  • Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection.
  • Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama.

Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate.

It was refreshing to just write C. It isn't pretty, but neither is Tailwind.

SQLite is a breath of fresh air.

I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to.

SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal.

## WHAT I WOULD CHANGE

CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library. This means you get very little out of the box.

You need to write your own utilities to handle things like:

  • Cookie parsing and creation.
  • Query parameter parsing and validation.
  • Form data parsing and validation.
  • Escaping input for display.

I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model.

I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries).

Maybe I'll publish cgi.h as a start.

## CONCLUSION

CGI is old, but it's not forgotten.

Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily.

And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade.

Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is a commercial product running on a single binary using a serving model that was officially standardized in 2004.

It has fewer moving parts than anything I've shipped before. I'll be reaching for this stack again.
