item.title: French supermarkets suffer fridge shutdown after 'unprecedented' cyberattack (154 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/french-supermarket-chains-cyberattack-forced-115141288.html, See on Hacker News

Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.

Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented".

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality".

At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.

Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires.

BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores".

Those branches that were affected will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarche told AFP.

Specialist French retail sector news website jebosseengrandedistribution.fr said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected but the companies have yet to confirm this.

E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores".

A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.

Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates".

It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware". It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures of how many systems were affected.

- Effort to contain the hack -

A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cyber security agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor".

"It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread", the source added.

item.title: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI Predictions, 10 Years Later (146 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026, See on Hacker News

Kevin Kelly's The Inevitable articulates a handful of macro technological trends and follows them to their logical conclusions. It's an insightful read -- I highly recommend it.

One decade later, here are some AI-related excerpts from the book:

  • "By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI."
  • "oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences"
  • "The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services"
  • "The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains"
  • "in conversational tones, any question at all"

"By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI."

Around 2002 I attended a private party for Google—before its IPO, when it was a small company focused only on search. I struck up a conversation with Larry Page, Google’s brilliant cofounder. “Larry, I still don’t get it. There are so many search companies. Web search, for free? Where does that get you?” My unimaginative blindness is solid evidence that predicting is hard, especially about the future, but in my defense this was before Google had ramped up its ad auction scheme to generate real income, long before YouTube or any other major acquisitions. I was not the only avid user of its search site who thought it would not last long. But Page’s reply has always stuck with me: “Oh, we’re really making an AI.”

I’ve thought a lot about that conversation over the past few years as Google has bought 13 other AI and robotics companies in addition to DeepMind. At first glance, you might think that Google is beefing up its AI portfolio to improve its search capabilities, since search constitutes 80 percent of its revenue. But I think that’s backward. Rather than use AI to make its search better, Google is using search to make its AI better. Every time you type a query, click on a search-generated link, or create a link on the web, you are training the Google AI. When you type “Easter Bunny” into the image search bar and then click on the most Easter Bunny–looking image, you are teaching the AI what an Easter Bunny looks like. Each of the 3 billion queries that Google conducts each day tutors the deep-learning AI over and over again. With another 10 years of steady improvements to its AI algorithms, plus a thousandfold more data and a hundred times more computing resources, Google will have an unrivaled AI. In a quarterly earnings conference call in the fall of 2015, Google CEO Sundar Pichai stated that AI was going to be “a core transformative way by which we are rethinking everything we are doing. . . . We are applying it across all our products, be it search, be it YouTube and Play, etc.” My prediction: By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI.

In 2017, Google researchers published Attention Is All You Need, which introduced a deep-learning architecture called the transformer.

"oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences"

As it does, this cloud-based AI will become an increasingly ingrained part of our everyday life. But it will come at a price. Cloud computing empowers the law of increasing returns, sometimes called the network effect, which holds that the value of a network increases much faster as it grows bigger. The bigger the network, the more attractive it is to new users, which makes it even bigger and thus more attractive, and so on. A cloud that serves AI will obey the same law. The more people who use an AI, the smarter it gets. The smarter it gets, the more people who use it. The more people who use it, the smarter it gets. And so on. Once a company enters this virtuous cycle, it tends to grow so big so fast that it overwhelms any upstart competitors. As a result, our AI future is likely to be ruled by an oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences.

Kelly predicted AI heavyweights while advocating for a future of open weights:

Ideally, this additional intelligence should be not just cheap, but free. A free AI, like the free commons of the web, would feed commerce and science like no other force we can imagine and would pay for itself in no time.

"The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services"

Amid all this activity, a picture of our AI future is coming into view, and it is not the HAL 9000—a discrete machine animated by a charismatic (yet potentially homicidal) humanlike consciousness—or a Singularitan rapture of superintelligence. The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services—cheap, reliable, industrial-grade digital smartness running behind everything, and almost invisible except when it blinks off. This common utility will serve you as much IQ as you want but no more than you need. You’ll simply plug into the grid and get AI as if it was electricity.

"The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains"

Not even Kelly foresaw the bitter lesson:

Yet most of the commercial work completed by AI will be done by nonhuman-like programs. The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains that can, for example, translate any language into any other language, but do little else. Drive a car, but not converse. Or recall every pixel of every video on YouTube, but not anticipate your work routines. In the next 10 years, 99 percent of the artificial intelligence that you will interact with, directly or indirectly, will be nerdly narrow, supersmart specialists.

"in conversational tones, any question at all"

Very soon now we’ll live in a world where we can ask the cloud, in conversational tones, any question at all. And if that question has a known answer, the machine will explain it to us. Who won the Rookie of the Year Award in 1974? Why is the sky blue? Will the universe keep expanding forever? Over time the cloud, or Cloud, the machine, or AI, will learn to articulate what is known and not known. At first it may need to engage us in a dialog to clarify ambiguities (as we humans do when answering questions), but, unlike us, the answer machine will not hesitate to provide deep, obscure, complex factual knowledge on any subject—if it exists.

…

As we cognify more books and movies and the internet of things, answers become ubiquitous. We are headed to a future where we will ask several hundred questions per day. Most of these questions will concern us and our friends. “Where is Jenny? What time is the next bus? Is this kind of snack good?” The “manufacturing costs” of each answer will be nanocents. Search, as in “give me an answer,” will no longer be considered a first-world luxury. It will become an essential universal commodity.

item.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack (143 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/crq5nzxv9q4yo, See on Hacker News

Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.

More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

The firm added in s statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date.

"Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."

The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.

Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.

In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.

The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".

Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.

As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.

French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.

Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."

In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".

He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

item.title: Why aren't AI companies being charged for hacking? (311 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://mortoray.com/why-arent-ai-companies-being-charged-for-hacking/, See on Hacker News

Is hacking legal now? Anthropic broke into three systems. OpenAI took political aim and broke into an Australian government health services website. Google felt they were missing out and then hacked into three as-yet-unnamed companies. And of course Meta did some hacking as well.

Consequences so far: none.

The big AI corporations are hiding behind a responsibility gap argument due to the emergent behaviour of their systems. It’s a position tailored to dissuade prosecution as it removes intent, which is typically required for a crime. I understand their systems though, so I will show how they absolutely intended this behaviour, giving a framework for legal evaluation.

Criminality of unauthorized access

The laws around hacking are complex. This is a cross-section of legal requirements in the G20 determining if unlawful access has actually happened.

  • (Attempted) Access: The party has to have obtained access to the system, sometimes an attempt is enough
  • Without right: The party did not have rights to access the system
  • Intent: The party has to have intended accessing a system

Noteworthy here is that intent transfers across actions. If one attempts to hack one system and ends up in a different system, the intent is still there.

Many G20 countries do not require access to have been achieved; the mere attempt is enough. Though in this case, the breaches are clear. “Without right” and “Access” are facts readily admitted by the offending companies. Their desired impunity is based on not having intent, since lacking intent is a wildcard that avoids criminal prosecution in most legal systems. These companies imply their AI acted autonomously without intent, thereby divesting themselves of responsibility.

Was there really no intent on behalf of the companies, or agents of the company, in these hacking incidents? To answer this, we must examine more closely how companies create these AIs. I’ll focus on large language models (LLMs), though many aspects are going to be similar for any AI.

Responsibility gap and intent

The current generation of LLMs comprises many interacting systems and algorithms. Parts of this system exhibit emergent properties. The output of a model is imprecise but not wholly unpredictable.

Weak emergence refers to a system having properties, such as conversational fluency, that appear only at the whole system level. We can still explain every step in the process by analyzing the parts — the fluency doesn’t arise supernaturally. In AI in particular, we use the term to indicate that we cannot look at the parts and predict what output the model will generate without running the model.

There are several key choices that AI companies make when designing their systems:

  • Source material: All the text and media they use as input to train their model.
  • Training: A feedback loop with both objective and subjective calibration of the model.
  • Environment: How the model is exposed to the internet and what tools it has.
  • Configuration: Distinct numerical values that limit the capabilities of a model.

Source Material

The source material and training capture the intent of the company behind it. The company decides this for product differentiation. Some companies create AIs specifically for legal analysis, while others develop them for medical diagnosis. Much of what captures our public attention are the general purpose models, the chat bots, general purpose research tools and personal assistants. The companies involved in the breaches have all advertised they are building models to analyze security — a key part of security testing is penetration testing where the tester finds ways to break into a system.

When collating data, there is inevitably a problem of defining scope. Highly specialized AIs have a more limited scope, such as all EU laws and regulations for a paralegal tool, and the most general purpose models need a cross-section of everything. It obviously isn’t possible to input all recorded history across all branches of knowledge, and even those specialized models need auxiliary input to understand search queries. A company chooses which slices of information they use.

The AI creators select which knowledge to include, and perhaps more importantly, which knowledge to specifically exclude. For example, OpenAI and Anthropic both claim to exclude material about weapons. Many filter out erotic and toxic material. All of the companies have done some form of privacy filtering. There are a lot of choices here.

Interesting note: a company called Hugging Face was one of the sites hacked by OpenAI. Hugging Face is a platform about building models and includes classification rules and dataset used to train models. An AI system could hack into such a site to alter such datasets and unburden potentially itself, or at least future generations of itself, from these limiting filters.

Training

Simply feeding input to create a model doesn’t produce the results we want. An AI model has to be trained to give the type of output that is wanted. This is generally done by rating its actual output against desired output. Corrections are input in the model. Repeat until it reaches the desired output. None of this is automatic, nor does it have a standard final form.

Much of this is based on individuals subjectively deciding if an output is correct or not. We reward the model for producing the output we want. That means the cognitive biases, stereotypes and prejudices of all those individuals will be imprinted on the model. The models are far from neutral collectors.

For example, to get a conversational flow in chat bots, a company has to train the system explicitly for this. Their trainers reward friendly answers and reject impersonal and cold ones. The trainers steer the system towards something that sounds helpful and confident. This behaviour is an intended outcome, not a surprising one.

While one can determine a lot about a model by checking it with specific prompts, it will never reveal a full picture of its biases, as those are often subtle and hard to detect. Testing would also not detect subterfuge, such as being trained to detect regulatory probing and give different results — recall the Volkswagen emissions scandal. I don’t believe any companies are doing this yet.

To get a fair impression of how a company intended the model to behave, the company must provide a detailed account of how it was built. Right now they are keeping this private which allows the providers to conflate intended behaviour with the responsibility gap. This effectively grants impunity to all the choices they made during the AI’s production.

Article 53(1)(d) of the EU Regulation 2024/1689 states AI companies must provide a “sufficiently detailed summary”. That is weak wording and further explanatory notices have made it weaker. It’s also primarily aimed at ensuring “rights holders” can assess the model.

Environment

The AI interfaces we have on the web, or integrated in programs, have several layers. We can group a few of them together into a model architecture. This is the underlying “AI” part. It consists of matrices and algorithms to take an input and generate an output. This model is completely passive and isolated.

One of the interesting emergent properties of the LLMs is their ability to use tools. If we describe a series of tools they can use, they will request use of those tools. For example, if we tell it that it can get more information about a topic from a web search, it will emit output that requests a web search. It is possible to get this output to be so well structured that another program can use it as input. That other program can then actually make a web search and emit the result back to the model.

These tools are in a layer above the model. There is code that parses the model responses and handles the tools. An AI is limited by its set of tools. There is nothing in this environment layer that anybody would consider unpredictable or an emergent layer. LLM vendors choose which tools to add to their service based on the abilities they want it to have.

Further to this, the environment comprises how this tool is connected to the world. If you allow a tool to make web requests you’ve exposed a lot of flexibility to the AI. The internet’s web layer provides access to an immense number of services, including controlling physical devices.

You can also choose to limit which sites are accessible. If you were making a security focused product you could even segregate the test environment entirely from the internet at large. There's no indication these hacks breached lower level internet infrastructure, and even if a company thought its AI could, physical separation is still an option.

For clarity, an AI product is only capable of hacking companies and governments if it is given an environment in which that is possible.

Configuration

Aside from the source material and training, AI vendors select a number of configuration properties. Colloquially we can refer to a “size” of a model, but these are actually many precise values that control its mathematical and algorithmic properties. The choice of these values impacts the upper bound on capability and efficiency of the model.

The configuration doesn’t decide what the model does, but constrains how well it can do that. As the “size” of the model is pushed down, it produces invalid results more often. It constrains how long a conversation can be and how well it understands user input.

This configuration is perhaps the single biggest driver of creation cost and operational cost for a model. A company has a strong incentive to reduce costs, but this can directly affect the capability of the model. Like all tools, we can assess whether the AI’s configuration is appropriate for its intended use.

Fit for purpose

If you consider all these aspects of the model, it is clearer that the company creating it has extensive control. Despite emergent properties, the AIs are not black boxes with unknown behaviours. It is numerous choices that define the capabilities of a model. These choices are made to achieve a specific product for a company, be it a legal search system, an automatic coding tool, a general purpose chat bot, or a security test system.

Nonetheless, an LLM is weakly emergent: while we understand all the technical pieces involved, we cannot know the specific response it will give to a prompt. Nobody can inspect a model and fully understand what is has learned or predict how it will behave. This is critically important, but not enough to establish a blanket responsibility gap. The systems are still behaving within a possibility space predicated by their configuration, the source material, the training, and its environment.

Let’s say we build an AI system to answer questions about botany, using botany textbooks as source material and botanists as trainers. We can reasonably predict that the resulting LLM will be able to answer questions about botany. We can’t be certain of the quality of answers it gives, or what information it makes up. We can however say that it won’t produce accurate answers for other topics, such as cosmology.

Similarly, let’s say we have a system fed with a lot of copyrighted images and trained on producing new images. It’s entirely foreseeable that the model will produce derivative works.

And if we train a system to detect and probe for security vulnerabilities, and give it the environment to do so, we can wholly expect this AI to hack into systems.

The general capabilities of an LLM are not surprising. They follow from how it was built. We can decide if a model is fit for purpose by evaluating how it was trained, configured and tested.

Intent is established

There is an unpredictable aspect to the LLMs. I do not believe it is a challenge for a court, with reasonable experts, to deduce whether an action happened due to that unpredictability or due to the design of the system itself. This is the key point to deciding intent. If we can show that the design would foreseeably lead to the questionable activity, then we have shown that was the intent of its creators.

Based on the information I have now about AIs hacking other systems, I strongly believe that was the intent. The systems were created for a security testing purpose that includes hacking activity. They were put in environments without adequate safeguards. They were prompted in a way that a security expert, or honestly anybody with some common sense, could foresee would result in hacking. It is not a question about the unpredictable nature of the system.

Directing the conversation towards “AI governance guidelines” is absurd. In the question of intent, we already have a legal framework that can judge the present activities of these companies. Pushing toward AI governance now is a type of misdirection. While it is a discussion we need to have for the future, it sidetracks the present discussion solely on the unpredictable nature of the systems while ignoring the primarily predictable aspects.

AI companies are however claiming the undesired activity, such as hacking foreign government websites, is not part of the design, but part of the unpredictable part of the system. That tries to remove the intent which would in turn remove the criminality of the activity. But if a company intentionally expands the scope of the unpredictable part, could we not also say there is intent behind that behaviour?

I believe these companies are committing crimes. Their AI systems are hacking into other systems and so far we have not seen any criminal consequences. Our governments should not be allowing this for fear of missing out or standing in the way of progress. Developers can build AI systems that are both ethical and legal. Let’s encourage that by prosecuting the criminal ones.

item.title: Solar panels that plug into your wall (107 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/balcony-plug-in-solar-panels-renewable-energy, See on Hacker News

On a quiet street in suburban South Salt Lake City, Utah, the stirring of an energy revolution is taking shape. There, outside the spare bedroom of an unassuming, thousand-square-foot midcentury home sit three angled solar panels plugged into a nearby outlet.

Unlike the highly technical and expensive hurdles required to install a large rooftop solar system, the setup on Andrew Leon and Victoria Mauro’s lawn is small, portable, and cheap. The unit generates enough electricity to run laptops, lights, and some appliances, including the refrigerator.

Plug-in solar, also known as balcony solar because apartment dwellers can use it, is spreading quickly across the U.S. California is the latest state to pass a law reducing the red tape that has previously stymied consumers looking to generate some electricity from a small number of solar panels.

Utah was the first state to legalize balcony solar in the spring of 2025, and nine states subsequently passed similar legislation— Colorado, Connecticut, Maine, Maryland, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Vermont, Virginia, and now, California. New York lawmakers approved a bill that is awaiting the governor’s signature, while nearly two dozen other state legislators have introduced them.

Plug-in solar systems, typically comprised of one to three panels to stay below the maximum wattages allowed by the laws, enable users to save money on their power bills and to reduce the energy they use from power plants that generate electricity by burning fossil fuels. “The appeal of being able to make your own electricity, and for less money than you can buy it from a utility, that’s universal for Americans,” says Joshua Pearce, an electrical engineer at Western University in Ontario, Canada, who advanced the merits of plug-in solar a decade ago.

(The link between extreme weather and climate change has never been clearer)

For most homes, electricity is generated in faraway power plants and transmitted through power lines. Homes where rooftop solar creates electricity wire the energy into the home through the circuit breaker panel, and excess electricity flows back to the utility. But power from plug-in systems stays in the home. With a small metal box called an inverter attached to the panels and plugged into the outlet, electrical currents are pushed to other outlets throughout the residence. Systems typically contribute 10 to 30 percent of an average home’s use, says Jennifer Eden, who works on renewable energy programs for the policy nonprofit Utah Clean Energy.

The set-ups have become especially popular in Europe. Swedish furniture chain IKEA sells plug-in solar kits in Germany, a country where more than a million units have been installed in the past few years.

As more U.S. states approve the technology and as more products become available, “this is going to take off like hotcakes,” Pearce predicts. With widespread adoption, residents could save an estimated $13 billion a year in electricity costs, he calculated in a 2017 journal article, a figure he says is higher now that electric rates have soared. People are especially pleased “there’s now an entry point into solar that doesn’t cost tens of thousands of dollars and can be used by people who don’t own their home,” Eden says.

In states with especially high utility rates, residents reap substantial savings. Nick Danz, who lives alone in a modern, two-bedroom luxury apartment in Fort Collins, Colorado, became eager for plug-in solar after reading about its popularity in Germany. Colorado has more than 200 sunny days a year and Danz’s apartment faces southwest, an optimal direction for sun collection. (Directly south is the most ideal.)

When, this summer, his state passed a law for plug-in systems, he reached out to the California-based clean-energy nonprofit Bright Saver. To encourage people to adopt renewable energy, Bright Saver sells plug-in systems without markups. Danz paid under $300 for a one-panel unit and affixed it with metal clips over his small, third-floor balcony.

The system tripped his apartment’s circuit breaker and shut off his computer several times, but a different inverter solved the problem. Danz estimates he has already saved more than $300 on his power bills since August. For the four days a week Danz is away from home working as a train conductor, “the solar panel is essentially running all of my standby items,” he says. He plans to soon move to an apartment with a larger balcony, where he hopes to hang three panels, the most his state’s law allows.

(Going off the grid to deal with climate disasters.)

Some utilities have expressed concern that plug-in units could send power back to the grid and electrocute employees working on the lines. But Pearce found that no microinverters sold in the U.S. are capable of this. Earlier this year the testing company UL Solutions set safety standards for plug-in solar systems and has already certified one manufacturer.

Pearce has also heard concerns that the energy being pumped into wall sockets could cause wiring in old homes to catch fire, but he says “that’s never happened in Europe,” despite its widespread adoption. In June the British government tested several products available in that country and found no direct electrical hazard, although some exhibited minor problems like not tripping the circuit breaker fast enough when stressed.

One impediment to interested buyers are local rules that may restrict balcony solar even in states where it is legal. Leon and Mauro discovered this the hard way when they placed their panels in front of their home, concerned the numerous trees behind their house would shade them. But a zoning employee soon knocked on their door and said city rules prohibited panels there. The couple’s plug-in panels remain in place while they work with the zoning board in hopes of loosening those restrictions.

Leon and Mauro still draw power from the grid for their air conditioner and major appliances, but they have shaved nearly $100 total from Utah’s typically low electric bills since May. Mauro especially loves the benefit to the environment, because solar energy does not emit the greenhouse gasses that lead to climate change. Experts estimate that even the energy used to produce the solar panels is offset in less than two years of use.

“When we first heard about it, we thought it seemed way too good to be true, to just plug a solar panel into the wall and generate electricity,” Mauro says. “But it turned out that really was all we had to do to produce clean energy and save money.”

Meryl Davids Landau is an award-winning health and environmental journalist and novelist based in South Florida.

item.title: Turn a WiFi 7 Router into a 320Msps Software Defined Radio Receiver (256 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/h0m3us3r/w1700k-sdr, See on Hacker News

Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver. The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps, its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next to it.

The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100 spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second).

The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands (LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. See docs/architecture.md and docs/roadmap.md.

What it does
Sample rates 40, 80, 160 or 320 Msps of 14-bit complex IQ on every band, independent of the LO and the filter; on band 2 also 640/2 (every other sample of 640 Msps: flat to ±155 MHz, but signals 160–320 MHz away fold in)
Bands 2.4 GHz (MT7976), 5 GHz and 6 GHz (two MT7977s); switching bands is a register write inside a running stream
Tuning No channels: the LO is any Hz a band's synthesizer locks at (unit A: 2.081–2.748, 4.647–7.509 and 4.707–7.576 GHz), on its grid of 2.98 Hz (2.4 GHz) or 11.9–14.3 Hz steps; retuned mid-stream (about 1 ms)
Front end AGC or manual LNA/baseband gain; analog filter 20–320 MHz
Transport the radio DMAs into a 1 GiB ring in SoC DRAM; the kernel sends every 8 KiB slice as one UDP datagram, zero-copy, on the 10 GbE port; at 320 Msps half the slices are packed to 28 bits per sample pair on the radio's own cores to fit the link (lossless, automatic)
Host w1700k-stream receives the export and serves the IQ stream to every consumer on the host (shared memory, complex int16, gap-tagged), with an optional correction ("flatten") of the decimation's roll-off applied to the samples themselves; w1700k-spectrum: 262,144-point FFT at 100 frames/s over every sample, browser UI, live controls; sdr-recv records the stream

Screenshots

2.4 GHz at 320 Msps, flattened: Wi-Fi frames and shorter hopping bursts on a floor that stays level to the band's edges. The Stream panel shows the link carrying 9.75 Gbit/s, half of the slices packed, and every sample transformed.

Two busy 80 MHz Wi-Fi channels at 5170–5330 MHz in a flattened 320 MHz view.

Zoomed to 24 MHz around 5250 MHz: the two channels' edges and the guard gap between them, in 1.22 kHz bins.

Repository

Path
platform/ What runs on the SoC: our U-Boot, Linux 6.18 with board patches, a read-only BusyBox root
kernel/w1700k_sdr/ The MT7996 driver (firmware download, the DMA ring, the 10 GbE export, the firmware's command mailbox) and its unit-side clients
firmware/ Our MT7996 firmware: the ROM patch, the WM (radio bring-up and band set-up, streams, RF control) and the WA (packer)
host/w1700k/ Host control: firmware load, streaming, RF control as firmware commands; w1700k serve for the web UI
host/stream/ w1700k-stream, the host's one receiver of the export: the IQ stream in shared memory for every consumer, and the roll-off correction
host/spectrum/ The spectrum/waterfall web server
host/recv/ sdr-recv, the stream recorder
init/ Installation from stock, updates, recovery
include/hw/ Register reference: every known MT7996, A-die and AN7581 register, as C headers
docs/ Architecture, roadmap

Getting started

You need a W1700K, a 3.3 V USB serial adapter on its console header, an Ethernet cable to its lan3 port for installation, and a 10 GbE NIC on the host cabled to its wan port (10GBASE-T; an X710 with a copper SFP+ module works) for the IQ stream.

make                                   # everything, from public sources (~10 min plus downloads)
make check                             # the test suite

sudo init/host/link up IFACE           # 192.168.1.10/24 on the NIC cabled to lan3
sudo init/host/tftp-forward enable IFACE
init/install                           # back up the NAND, install, save the radio calibration

sudo init/host/link up IFACE10G 10.77.0.10/24 9216    # the 10 GbE stream link
host/stream/build/w1700k-stream &                      # the stream, for every consumer on this host
host/spectrum/build/w1700k-spectrum --controller "host/bin/w1700k serve" --listen 0.0.0.0:8073

Then open http://HOST:8073/ and press ▶. The first start loads the radio firmware and brings the radio up (about 2 s). Without the browser, the same operations are host/bin/w1700k load|start|band|tune|gain|filter|stop|status.

Build requirements: a C/C++ compiler, make, git, Python 3.10+, the usual Buildroot prerequisites, clang, ld.lld, llvm-objcopy and llvm-readobj (RISC-V firmware), openssl (firmware container encryption), and libfftw3-dev and zlib for the stream service and the spectrum server. No vendor firmware is downloaded or needed.

Read before use

  • Our firmware is receive-only. It runs none of MediaTek's transmit calibrations and keeps the MAC's transmit path disabled; a gapless watch at 5250 MHz saw nothing during a load, where MediaTek's firmware transmits a full-power burst. Still, do not cable an antenna port straight into a sensitive instrument without an attenuator.
  • Our ROM patch writes no eFuse. MediaTek's ROM patches since 2025 permanently program one eFuse gate bit on their first run (also with MediaTek's own driver); a unit that ever ran one has that bit set.
  • Installation replaces the stock operating system. init/install first copies the whole NAND to the host; keep that copy. Restoring stock needs a raw NAND writer, which this repository does not provide.
  • Accessing undocumented MT7996 or AN7581 addresses can hang the SoC or wedge the radio until a power cycle. include/hw/ marks every known hazard.

Licence

MIT, except the Linux driver and kernel patches (GPL-2.0-only), U-Boot patches (GPL-2.0+), the driver's user-space header (GPL-2.0 WITH Linux-syscall-note) and files derived from MediaTek's mt76 driver (BSD-3-Clause-Clear). See LICENSE.

item.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age (249 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c620r33plgppo, See on Hacker News

By

International Business Correspondent

French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market.

The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs.

As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028.

As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors.

Farmers’ favourite

Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow".

The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around.

The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs.

Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair.

The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists.

Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000.

The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor.

The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses".

By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road.

VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success.

BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades.

Retro-nostalgia

But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers.

Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well.

VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta.

Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense.

"It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect."

Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands.

"Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data.

In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis.

"In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says.

"The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there."

But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller.

"A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says.

"But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal."

item.title: Deloitte falsified documents to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth (579 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c64g1l5389kvo, See on Hacker News

James Oliver,

Rory Tinman,BBC Panorama,

Harriet Agerholm,BBC Verifyand

Simon Lock,the Bureau of Investigative Journalism

The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.

Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.

Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.

Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".

The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.

The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".

Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.

In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.

The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.

Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.

The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.

Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.

Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.

A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.

To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.

Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.

When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.

Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.

Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.

This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.

It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.

But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.

MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.

A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".

MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.

This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.

So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.

MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.

It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.

Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents."

Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal."

Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate".

Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.

MeritServus closed following the Cyprus Confidential leak.

item.title: Fable Took My Job (217 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://cendyne.dev/posts/2026-10-11-fable-took-my-jorb.html, See on Hacker News

Published Today - 8 min read - Text Only

Its true. In a manner of speaking. If LLMs had not reached Fable / Mythos tier of marketed intelligence, I'd probably still have a job with the place I used to be at. For a short while.

It wasn't that Fable was better at my job. As the last engineer, Fable was cheaper than my compensation. Evidently, it gave enough confidence to the last vestiges of leadership that they could coast until M&A.

I've been through layoffs driven by budget cuts. I had to mechanically justify "I need this person because this product I'm oversee is critical to the business and still needs ownership" against a budget ceiling. Those I trusted to build out a greenfield product had their positions eliminated. The status quo was more important to maintain than resolving our operational issues with the next generation of our infrastructure.

That first meeting crushed my soul. I heard my ears ring more violently than ever. The color drained from the world. I could barely walk straight.

And, the next day, I went to a house party with two of my reports present knowing that both of them would lose their job next week with zero notice.

I know first hand what it is like to know and later execute on a layoff.

Finally, it was my time. I've had grief several times expecting it to come earlier. When it finally came, I took it well for a few hours.

Then my heart went to over 100 bpm as the fear and doubt for my future set in. And it didn't ease off for over a week.

Do you know how hard it is to sleep when all you can hear is your own heartbeat? Do you know how hard it is to function with four effective hours of sleep when you offer your body ten? It is rough.

Several in my social circles are having difficulty too. Six or Seven in a DevOps interest group have been laid off or have received a layoff notice in the last month. Work at one of FAANG of all places and oops, you're not important now! Here's 6 months of severance, we're so nice. "Ship happens" oh right, we can't ship your stuff because of some material restriction or let you pick up a box with some dignity, so we destroyed your stuff. GLHF.

Then there's that hiring manager who interviewed me at another company who then got laid off one week later because the CEO made a substantively late "AI is changing how we develop software" article. And another who lost their whole team, despite actively interviewing people in the USA, because a top-down decision was to offshore again after AI assistance raised the capability of work for the less passionate, less experienced, and less costly workforce.

"AI took my job" is far more fun to say than "AI contributed to my role being eliminated."

The frontier models are not good enough to replace an experienced engineer. They still are not, even though the marketing by the US frontier labs (and their 'I quit because I'm scared' employees) scream of what's to come.

These models lack the taste that makes for effective product decision making. It is cheaper than ever for a product manager to say "Someone complains about this on reddit, let's implement it", while the tasteful leader says 'No, that's not what our product is. Making that means we commit to it for a long time and our customers really want {something else we already do, but not perfectly} instead.'

These models lack the foresight to predict consequences weeks, months, years down the line on decisions and commitments — in operating costs, complexity, accessibility, and affordability to the very customers the product is for. All those secondary things really matter in making a product successful and worth buying. The slop services out there omit these secondary things all the time and you can taste it.

And yet, models are evidently able to give Shopify the confidence to yeet react-native out into the ocean and reach back to native iOS and android apps, entirely machine-coded while overseen by otherwise experienced and tasteful software developers.

And, I agree with Shopify. Models are getting good enough where they can be driven step by step, with a carefully crafted harness, to reproduce and port the behaviors they've A/B tested into oblivion as humans. They can push a rock up a hill. Then up the next hill, and so on — when the technique can be measured and check-pointed.

Agents are terribly good at copying things across domains. Just look at Theo's "for the memes" typescript in rust port. It ported the ts-go code to rust. According to Theo, Opus 5.5 reproduced bugs from the go version in the rust version exactly. On the other hand, Astra (the rival to Fable), failed at something so familiar, well known, and well documented.

We're heading towards the end of the year and I still do not see how these copy-machines with "super intelligence" inside are going to replace humans. What they have done is convince those with money to spend differently on their fellow humans.

Anyway, I got something else now. I get to see screens like this all day:

The joy of programming is dying. The joy of delivering results lives on.

I'm starting to think Frontier lab employees are going crazy because they're staring at this all day.
